Activation steering works by adding a direction vector to a model's residual stream to amplify or suppress a concept — but this assumes concept representations are cleanly separable in activation space, which they aren't. The central question is: when you steer toward concept A, how much do you inadvertently activate concept B, C, or D that share the same neurons in a superposed, polysemantic encoding? A beginner assumes that because two concepts have different steering vectors, they're orthogonal enough to steer independently; an expert knows that in high-dimensional but overcomplete representations, vectors can have small cosine similarity yet still substantially overlap in the subspace spanned by the polysemantic neurons that do the actual computational work. The worry isn't the dot product between two steering vectors in the full residual stream — it's that both vectors load heavily onto the same small cluster of neurons, so the effective interference in the functionally active subspace is much larger than the global geometry suggests. Concretely, if neuron 847 responds to both "French language" and "royalty" (a documented polysemanticity pattern), then a "translate to French" steering vector and a "describe as noble" steering vector will cross-activate each other through that neuron in ways that aggregate interference analyses completely miss.

The deeper problem is that superposition geometry itself may shift across contexts because attention modulates which features are active, meaning the polysemantic neuron subspace relevant to your steering vectors is not fixed — it's a function of the prompt, so interference measured at one context is measuring a moving target.
